items.stem:
Read the extract.

Unilever adopted zero-based budgeting from 2015, aiming to save about €2 bn over three years by justifying spending from scratch.

Explain why budgets can sometimes demotivate employees. Refer to the extract or to another organization you have studied. [4]
items.answer: If budgets are imposed without consultation or set unrealistically, staff may feel they cannot meet targets; inflexible budgets can also prevent sensible spending.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why dividing a business into profit centres can motivate managers.
items.answer: Managers are responsible for their own centre's results, which gives them clear targets, autonomy and recognition when they perform well. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Managers are responsible for their own centre's results, which gives them clear targets, autonomy and recognition when they perform well. items.stem: Briefly describe Unilever's cost-saving programme and explain what it reveals about budgeting methods.
items.answer: Unilever adopted zero-based budgeting from 2015, aiming to save about €2 bn over three years by justifying spending from scratch. Requiring every cost to be justified can cut waste but is time-consuming and may discourage innovation
items.markingKey: Context (Unilever adopted zero-based budgeting from 2015, aiming to save about €2 bn over three years by justifying spending from scratch.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: A student claims: "Budgets are only useful for the finance department." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Budgets coordinate all departments, set targets for marketing, operations and HR, and help allocate resources across the business.

A financial plan of expected revenues and costs for a future period, used to set targets and control spending

items.stem: Briefly explain why budgets can improve control in a business.
items.answer: Managers can compare actual results with planned figures, identify variances, and take corrective action, and budget holders are accountable for their spending.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a profit centre and a cost centre.
items.answer: A cost centre is a part of the business to which only costs are allocated; a profit centre has both costs and revenues allocated, so its profit can be measured.
items.markingKey: A cost centre is a part of the business to which only costs are allocated; a profit centre has both costs and revenues allocated, so its profit can be measured. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: The managers of a garden centre treat each department as a profit centre. Last quarter: plants: revenue £60,000, direct costs £66,000; tools: revenue £200,000, direct costs £190,000; café: revenue £80,000, direct costs £88,000. Calculate the profit of each profit centre and the total, and explain one reason why the business might keep the weakest centre (café) open.

items.stem: Tasman Surf Co. must choose whether to open a flagship store (cost €80,000) or invest in e-commerce (cost €90,000). If it chooses to open a flagship store, there is a 60% chance of success with returns of €300,000 and a 40% chance of returns of €60,000. If it chooses to invest in e-commerce, there is a 80% chance of returns of €180,000 and a 20% chance of €50,000. Calculate the expected value of each option, net of its cost, and state which option is preferred.
items.answer: Open a flagship store: EV = €204,000, net €124,000; invest in e-commerce: EV = €154,000, net €64,000. Preferred: open a flagship store.
items.markingKey: EV = Σ(probability × outcome): 0.6 × 300,000 + 0.4 × 60,000 = 204,000; 0.8 × 180,000 + 0.2 × 50,000 = 154,000; subtract costs. [M1] for a correct formula/method with substituted values; [A1] for both net EVs. Units (%, $, days, times) required for [A1]. Apply own figure rule (OFR) to later parts.

items.stem: Saffron Spice Co. is considering switching to 100% recycled packaging. A force field analysis scores driving forces – customer demand (3), staff support (2), government incentives (3) – and restraining forces – disruption to production (2), uncertain returns (3), lack of skills (3) (scores out of 5). Calculate the total for each side and state what the analysis suggests. Suggest one way to reduce the strongest restraining force.
items.answer: Driving forces = 8; restraining forces = 8. Restraining forces are at least as strong, so the change is unlikely to succeed without action. Strongest restraint: uncertain returns – reduce it through consultation, training or phased implementation.
items.markingKey: [1] driving total 8; [1] restraining total 8; [1] conclusion; [1] relevant way to reduce the strongest restraining force.

items.stem: Saffron Spice Co. must choose whether to advertise on TV (cost €100,000) or run a social media campaign (cost €30,000). If it chooses to advertise on TV, there is a 70% chance of success with returns of €300,000 and a 30% chance of returns of €40,000. If it chooses to run a social media campaign, there is a 50% chance of returns of €220,000 and a 50% chance of €70,000. Calculate the expected value of each option, net of its cost, and state which option is preferred.
items.answer: Advertise on TV: EV = €222,000, net €122,000; run a social media campaign: EV = €145,000, net €115,000. Preferred: advertise on TV.
items.markingKey: EV = Σ(probability × outcome): 0.7 × 300,000 + 0.3 × 40,000 = 222,000; 0.5 × 220,000 + 0.5 × 70,000 = 145,000; subtract costs.
